intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself against the questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What Gender Mainstreaming Is
sections.big_idea: Mainstreaming is **a process of assessing the effect on women and men of every planned action**, with equality as the goal.
in_plain_words: The ECOSOC definition of 1997 reads like a legal text because each clause closes an evasion. It covers any planned action, in all areas and at all levels, and makes gender a dimension of design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. Beijing 1995 made it the agreed strategy across 12 critical areas of concern.

The practical test is the deletion test: remove the gender paragraph and see whether anything else in the document changes. If nothing moves, gender was an annex. A gender-blind design assumes a user with a man's time, mobility and assets, and it excludes whoever does not fit.

Programmes sit on a ladder from exploitative to norm-changing, and mainstreaming aims upward. It is a policy obligation under CEDAW, the SDGs and national policy, and it uses equity to reach equality. Myths about adding women or running a separate project keep the work small.

levels.label: Norm-changing
levels.sub: aims to change norms and power

diagram.caption: the spectrum, best at the top

key_terms.meaning: Assessing the effect on women and men of any planned action, in all areas and levels.
Treating women and men as if their needs and constraints were identical.
The top rung of the ladder: aims to change unequal norms and power.
Allocating by need to reach a fair outcome.
Adopted by 189 governments in 1995; 12 critical areas.

worked_example.title: Place four programmes on the ladder
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's test for each approach.
steps: A community scheme assumes women will give unpaid labour and attend meetings for free. It relies on women's unpaid time, so it is exploitative.
A toilet block with no lockable facilities for women: gender was not considered, so it is gender-blind.
A training scheme that moves sessions to times women can attend adapts delivery to constraints, so it is sensitive.
A programme with a norms objective and a way to measure norms is norm-changing.

mistakes: Treating mainstreaming as adding women or counting female heads.
Writing a separate gender annex and calling the design mainstreamed.
Claiming the top rung of the ladder without a norms objective or a way to measure norms.
Describing it as a one-off activity instead of an ongoing process.

recall.q: Who coined the working definition, and when?
recall.a: UN ECOSOC, in its 1997 agreed conclusions.

recall.q: How many governments adopted the Beijing Platform for Action?
What is the quick diagnostic for an add-on?
recall.a: Delete the gender paragraph and see whether anything else changes.

recall.q: Which Indian articles does the deck cite for equality and special provision?
recall.a: Article 14 for equality and Article 15(3) for special provision for women and children.

recall.q: Why is the exploitative category easy to skip?
recall.a: It includes programmes that rely on women's unpaid labour, which are common.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.big_idea: Gender is **social and changeable**, and the concepts of role, need, condition, position and intersection tell you what to change.
in_plain_words: Sex is biological and gender is socially assigned, which means gendered outcomes are a legitimate object of policy. Moser names three kinds of women's work: productive, reproductive and community. Two of the three are invisible to national accounts, so time-use surveys matter.

Practical gender needs ease daily life and arise from existing roles. Strategic needs change women's position. In the same way, condition is a woman's material state and position is her standing relative to men. A handpump improves condition, and land in her name shifts position.

Kabeer's empowerment runs from resources to agency to achievements. Intersectionality means a woman's experience depends on caste, class, religion, disability, age and location. Gender also covers men and boys, and transgender and non-binary people.

key_terms.meaning: Productive, reproductive and community work carried at once.
Immediate needs that arise from existing roles.
Needs to change women's subordinate position.
Material state, and standing relative to men.
Overlapping disadvantages that are not simply additive.

worked_example.title: Condition or position?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's table of interventions.
steps: A new handpump improves her condition and leaves her position unchanged.
A cash transfer to her account improves condition and partly shifts position.
Land title in her name does both.
A panchayat seat with a budget shifts position and improves condition indirectly.
worked_example.answer: Handpump: condition only; transfer: condition and partly position; title: both; seat: position.

mistakes: Treating sex and gender as the same, which hides that gendered outcomes can change.
Adding a meeting or training to a woman's day as if time were free.
Describing a handpump as empowerment.
Reporting a gender gap and a caste gap separately and missing the intersection.

recall.q: What are Moser's three kinds of women's work?
Which two roles are invisible to national accounts?
What are Kabeer's three dimensions of empowerment?
Which court judgment recognised a third gender in India?
Whose term is intersectionality in the deck?

sections.title: Analytical Frameworks
sections.big_idea: A framework is a set of questions, so **pick the one that fits the task** and combine them.
in_plain_words: The Harvard framework (1985) maps activities and the access to and control over resources. It is quick and concrete but says little about why power is unequal. Moser asks whether a programme only eases life or reshapes power. Kabeer's Social Relations Approach looks at four institutions: household, market, state and community.

Parker's Gender Analysis Matrix is run by the community and fills four levels (women, men, household, community) against labour, time, resources and culture. Its useful output is the unexpected negative cell, a source of backlash.

The frameworks carry different politics, so choosing is an analytical decision. In practice teams use a hybrid. Four questions form the portable core: who does what, who has what, who decides, who benefits.

key_terms.meaning: Maps activities, access and control, and influencing factors.
Uses the triple role and practical or strategic needs.
Analyses inequality in household, market, state and community.
A participatory grid of four levels by four impact dimensions.
Who does, has, decides and benefits.

worked_example.title: Choose the framework
worked_example.setup: Match each question to the deck's recommended tool.
steps: What is the current pattern? Harvard.
Will this shift power or only ease life? Moser.
Why does this gap persist? Kabeer's SRA, which points at institutions you may not touch.
What will the community say changes? GAM.
worked_example.answer: Harvard, Moser, Kabeer and GAM; for all in a week, Harvard plus Moser and then validate.

mistakes: Treating the frameworks as interchangeable when they answer different questions.
Applying Harvard and then writing a claim about changing power on top of it.
Stopping at Harvard when the question is why the division of labour exists.
Skipping the third and fourth questions because they need survey items or conversations.

recall.q: When was the Harvard framework developed?
What are the four institutions in Kabeer's SRA?
What are the four impact dimensions in GAM?
Which book sets out Moser's framework?
Which data answers 'who does what'?

sections.title: Doing Gender Analysis
sections.big_idea: Gender analysis is the first step and not a luxury: **disaggregate, map who controls, and do it before the design is fixed**.
in_plain_words: Gender analysis examines roles, needs, constraints, opportunities and power, and predicts what a programme will do. An analysis commissioned after approval can only annotate the design. Sex-disaggregated data is step zero, because an average can hide a wide gap.

Gender data goes further than splitting existing indicators by sex. It measures unpaid care, violence, mobility and agency, and it uses methods that reach women. The four questions reveal wrong answers that treat the household as one unit.

Access is the opportunity to use a resource, and control is the power to decide over it. Women often have access without control. A lightweight analysis can be done in days: baseline data, separate focus groups for women and men, separate needs, a four-question test, a do-no-harm paragraph.

key_terms.meaning: Every indicator split by sex.
Data on gendered issues such as unpaid care, violence and agency.
The opportunity to use a resource.
The power to decide over a resource: sell, lease or keep the income.
A written risk section with actions.

worked_example.title: An average that hides a gap
worked_example.setup: The deck's example: an overall figure of 70% covered with men at 85% and women at 55%.
steps: Add the two: 85 + 55 = 140.
Average them: 140 ÷ 2 = 70, which is the headline figure.
The gap: 85 − 55 = 30 percentage points.
Report both rates, since the average hides a 30-point gap.
worked_example.answer: The headline 70% hides a 30-point gender gap.

mistakes: Offering 'we disaggregate by sex' as a complete answer.
Running one mixed focus group, which produces the men's account of the division of labour.
Asking about the household instead of individuals, such as 'does the family own land'.
Counting accounts opened and ignoring who operates them.

recall.q: What does gender analysis predict?
recall.a: What a policy or programme will do to women, men and gender-diverse people.

recall.q: What is the difference between access and control?
recall.a: Access is opportunity to use; control is power to decide.

recall.q: Why run women's and men's groups separately?
recall.a: Mixed groups systematically produce the men's account.

recall.q: What is the minimum for baseline data?
What does the deck call the bedrock of gender analysis?

sections.title: Gender Across the Programme Cycle
sections.big_idea: A gap at any stage **leaks the gains made at the others**, so ask the gender question at every stage.
in_plain_words: Analysis, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation each have a gender question. The commonest leak sits between design and implementation. Design decisions such as meeting time, location, staff, information channel and eligibility documents have predictable gendered effects.

In delivery, pair each barrier with its fix: women set the schedule, deliver closer, recruit women staff, use channels women control, and provide childcare. Monitoring should disaggregate every result and add indicators on control, voice and workload.
Gender markers score projects from 0 to 2 and are self-assigned. Participation has levels from nominal to authority, and a do-no-harm lens guards against backlash with referral routes in place.

key_terms.meaning: A score of how strongly a project advances gender equality.
Names on a list, attendance only.
A husband attending in his wife's place.
Anticipating backlash, with a referral route ready.
Management information system, where disaggregation is built in.

worked_example.title: Score three projects
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's tests: 0 means no gender analysis informed the design, 1 means analysis changed something concrete, 2 means the project would not exist without the gender objective.
steps: A road built with no gender analysis scores 0.
A road plus safe transport for women, because analysis changed the design, scores 1.
A programme to end gender-based violence would not exist without the gender objective, so 2.
A maternal-health programme serving women scores 2 only if it aims to change gendered outcomes.
worked_example.answer: 0, 1, 2, and 2 only with a gendered-outcome aim.

mistakes: Scoring 2 because women are the beneficiaries.
Counting '50% of attendees were women' as participation.
Holding meetings in the care-heavy hours and then recording low attendance by women.
Publishing names or amounts locally for a transfer to women.

recall.q: What are the five levels of participation in the deck?
recall.a: Nominal, present, voice, influence and authority.

recall.q: Which intervention has the clearest evidence and lowest adoption?
What does the score-2 test ask?
recall.a: Would the project still make sense with the gender objective removed?

recall.q: What is the red flag at portfolio level?
recall.a: Lots of 1s, almost no 2s and a pile of unscored 0s.

recall.q: When can a leak still be fixed?
recall.a: In monitoring, for example by monthly disaggregated participation data.

sections.title: Gender-Responsive Budgeting
sections.big_idea: Budgets are policy stated in money, so **follow the money for the whole budget**, revenue and spending.
in_plain_words: GRB analyses and restructures the whole budget to assess its effect on gender equality. It covers revenue as well as expenditure, and it applies to mainstream schemes as well as women-specific ones. Sort spending into three buckets: women-specific, pro-equality within general, and general.

India's Gender Budget Statement has been in the Union Budget since 2005-06. Part A holds schemes with 100% allocation for women and girls, Part B schemes with at least 30%, and from 2024-25 Part C lists pro-women schemes below 30%. It rests on ministry self-reporting. Most spending that decides a woman's day sits in states and local bodies.

The five-step method runs from profiling to reallocating, and step 4, tracking spending by gender, is the hinge. Watch for reporting without budgeting, mislabelling, allocation without release and no outcome link.

key_terms.meaning: Analysis and restructuring of the whole budget through a gender lens.
Statement 13 in India's Union Budget since 2005-06.
The planned allocation.
What was released and spent.
Tagging a general scheme as 'for women' to inflate the figure.

worked_example.title: Allocation without release
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a gender-tagged line has a budget estimate of Rs 200 crore and actuals of Rs 120 crore.
steps: The gap: 200 − 120 = 80 crore.
As a share of the estimate: 80 ÷ 200 = 0.4, or 40%.
The deck says to compare budget estimates, revised estimates and actuals for gender-tagged lines.
A 40% shortfall means the allocation overstates what women received.
worked_example.answer: Rs 80 crore, or 40%, was never spent.

mistakes: Treating GRB as a separate women's budget.
Looking only at spending and forgetting revenue.
Counting allocations in the Statement as verified spending.
Stopping at step 3, where the budget is checked against the policy.

recall.q: What does GRB cover beyond expenditure?
Who developed the five-step GRB framework in the deck?
What does Part B of the Gender Budget Statement hold?
recall.a: Schemes with at least 30% allocation for women.

recall.q: Which Kerala programme is the longest-running example?
recall.a: The Women Component Plan in local planning.

recall.q: What is the hinge step in GRB?

sections.title: Indicators & Measuring Change
sections.big_idea: Measure **three layers of change** with disaggregated indicators and pair every number with a narrative.
in_plain_words: What goes unmeasured goes unfunded, but what is easy to measure gets over-funded. Most unmeasurable gender outcomes have a measurable proxy that nobody specified. The deck's three layers are access or condition, agency, and position or norms, which move over months, years and decades.

Agency indicators from NFHS cover who decides on healthcare and major purchases, visits to family, phone use and an account she herself uses. Violence measurement needs private interviews, trained women interviewers and referral pathways. Composite indices hide which dimension is failing.

Good indicators are disaggregable, relevant, sensitive, ethical and feasible. Numbers and narratives work together: Most Significant Change and outcome harvesting let women define change. Collect the qualitative data before you know the quantitative result.

diagram.caption: three layers, from slowest to fastest

key_terms.meaning: Measures decision-making and voice.
A measurable proxy for something hard to count.
UNDP Gender Inequality Index.
Measures gaps and leaves out levels.
Collecting stories of change, then deciding collectively which matter.

worked_example.title: Accounts opened versus accounts operated
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 500 accounts are opened for women, and holders operate 200 of them.
steps: Accounts opened is the easy count: 500.
Accounts operated by the holder: 200.
Share operated: 200 ÷ 500 = 0.4, or 40%.
The access number says 500, and the agency number says 40%.
worked_example.answer: 40% of the accounts are operated by their holders.

mistakes: Reporting on the first layer and claiming the third.
Reporting benefits at household level.
Reading a rank in an index as a diagnosis.
Reading rising violence reports as always rising violence, when disclosure may have improved.

recall.q: What are the three indicator layers?
recall.a: Access or condition, agency, and position or norms.

recall.q: Which layer moves in decades?
What are the five properties of a useful gender indicator?
recall.a: Disaggregable, relevant, sensitive, ethical and feasible.

recall.q: Why interview in private on violence?
What test do you apply to an indicator?
recall.a: What value it would take if the programme succeeded and if it failed.

sections.title: The Twin-Track Approach
sections.big_idea: Run **mainstreaming and targeted empowerment together**, because each track covers the other's blind spot.
in_plain_words: Mainstreaming alone can dilute into nothing, and women-only projects alone stay marginal. The twin-track approach runs both at once and is standard in EU, UN and most donor policy. Track 1 integrates gender into every policy, programme and budget. Track 2 runs dedicated empowerment interventions.

The failures are mirror images. Mainstreaming alone becomes everyone's job and so no one's, and targeting alone leaves the mainstream blind. Track 2 examples include SHGs, girls' scholarships, women-only skilling and reserved seats. A caution: one women's project does not mean gender is done.

The mix shifts by context. Where gaps are wide and voice is weak, Track 2 may lead to build capability, and Track 1 then opens opportunity. A third strand works with men and boys on shared care and masculinities, with sustained group work.

key_terms.meaning: Integrating gender into every policy, programme and budget.
Dedicated women's empowerment interventions.
Targeted work becoming the place where all gender work is sent.
Track 2 builds capability; Track 1 opens opportunity.
Reserved one-third of local seats for women.

worked_example.title: Weight the mix by context
steps: Wide gaps and weak voice: Track 2 first, to build agency.
Gaps narrowing and women organised: Track 1, to open the mainstream.
Strong policy but weak delivery: Track 1 with accountability.
Backlash rising: both tracks, with do-no-harm foregrounded.
worked_example.answer: Track 2, Track 1, Track 1 with accountability, and both with do-no-harm.

mistakes: Running one women's project and declaring gender done.
Treating targeting as a diversion from the mainstream.
Keeping no Track 2, so there is no home for specialist capacity.
Letting men become the visible voice of gender work.

recall.q: Why does mainstreaming alone fail?
recall.a: It dilutes to a checkbox and becomes everyone's job, so no one's.

recall.q: Why does targeting alone fail?
recall.a: It stays a marginal silo and the mainstream stays blind.

recall.q: What did the 73rd Amendment achieve?
recall.a: Over a million women in local government within a decade.

recall.q: What is the sequencing logic?
recall.a: Track 2 builds capability to claim space and Track 1 creates the space.

recall.q: What do work with men and boys aim to remove?

sections.title: Institutionalising Gender
sections.big_idea: Gender is institutionalised when it **survives the committed individual leaving**.
in_plain_words: Institutionalisation embeds gender into policy, systems, skills, budget and culture so that it becomes the default. A gender policy must be wired into the gateways: no gender analysis, no approval. Procurement and partnership criteria are the most underused lever.

Capacity means training for all staff, required tools, time in the workplan, a budget and an accountable person. A gender focal point needs seniority, a mandate and resources, or the role de-mainstreams gender by making it one person's burden.

Accountability has four mechanisms: targets in performance plans, mandatory disaggregated reporting, marker tracking and consequences tied to results. Only the last changes behaviour. A gender audit turns the lens inward, culture is measurable through records, and leadership signals decide effort.

key_terms.meaning: Embedding gender in policy, systems, skills, budget and culture.
A person who advises and builds capacity, with seniority and resources.
A participatory self-assessment of how well gender is mainstreamed.
Targets, reporting and consequences tied to results.
Requires an Internal Committee and annual reporting for qualifying workplaces.

worked_example.title: Is this organisation institutionalised?
worked_example.setup: Apply the deck's tests to four findings.
steps: A policy exists but approval is never blocked: the policy layer fails the test.
The MIS accepts undisaggregated records: the systems layer fails.
Only the gender team has been trained: the skills layer fails.
The work stopped when the champion left: the culture layer fails.
worked_example.answer: None of the four layers passes; the organisation has hired one committed person.

mistakes: Describing a policy that cannot block an approval as institutionalisation.
Appointing a junior woman as focal point with no authority or budget.
Treating training alone as enough.
Running an audit with no management response or follow-up date.

recall.q: What is the real test of institutionalisation?
Which accountability mechanism has teeth?
What two fixes help the focal point role?
recall.a: Time in the job description and formal sign-off in approvals.

recall.q: Who pioneered the participatory gender audit?
Which statute gives culture a floor on harassment?

sections.title: Challenges & Critiques
sections.big_idea: Mainstreaming is near-universal in language and patchy in practice; **name which critique applies**.
in_plain_words: Five critiques are distinct diagnoses with distinct remedies: policy evaporation, tokenism, depoliticisation, co-option and capacity failure. Longwe's evaporation image is commitment draining away like water in heat at each handover down the bureaucracy, so that little survives into implementation.

Tokenism keeps the form: a paragraph, a photograph, a quota on paper. The depoliticisation critique says tools and markers strip out the political core, and co-option shows in language shifts from women to gender and from rights to efficiency. Capacity failures have cheap structural fixes.

Resistance is real, open and quiet, and quiet non-compliance is beaten by verification. To keep mainstreaming honest, keep power in the frame, resource the work or admit it is rhetoric, track outcomes and keep women's movements at the table.

key_terms.meaning: Longwe's term for commitments that vanish as they pass down the bureaucracy.
Gender addressed by form: a paragraph, a photograph, a quota.
Turning mainstreaming into technical tools that strip out the power question.
Draining the feminist politics from gender work.
Passive resistance, beaten by verification.

worked_example.title: Name the critique
steps: A strong policy at headquarters with almost nothing on the ground is policy evaporation.
A gender paragraph in the proposal that changed nothing is tokenism.
A checklist that counts women and never asks who decides is the technical turn.
A donor template that asks for 'efficiency' and drops 'rights' shows co-option.

mistakes: Collapsing the critiques into a general complaint that mainstreaming failed.
Waiting for attitude change when a structural fix is available.
Wishing resistance away instead of anticipating it.
Reporting the training count and not the gap.

recall.q: Who coined 'policy evaporation'?
Where can a commitment evaporate?
recall.a: At each handover: policy to strategy, strategy to budget, budget to workplan, workplan to delivery, delivery to reporting.

recall.q: What is the lever against tokenism?
Which argument risks defeat by evidence about payoff?
What defeats quiet non-compliance?
recall.a: Verification, by making it a checked requirement.

sections.title: The India Context & Practice
sections.big_idea: India has dense gender machinery and uneven outcomes, so **implementation is the binding constraint**.
in_plain_words: India's machinery spans constitutional guarantees (Articles 14, 15, 16, 39, 42), the Ministry of Women and Child Development, the Gender Budget Statement since 2005-06, the 73rd and 74th Amendments and laws such as POSH, the Domestic Violence Act and the Maternity Benefit Act. Nearly every demand has a domestic hook to cite.

Flagship schemes mix tracks: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and DAY-NRLM are targeted, PM Ujjwala meets practical needs, and MGNREGA carries a 33% share for women. Reforms such as NEP 2020, the labour codes and the 2017 maternity amendment show who bears the cost of a gender measure.

Women's low labour-force participation is the sharpest gap. Panchayat reservation put over a million women into local government, but the sarpanch pati problem shows a seat is access and not control. A twelve-question checklist closes the course.

key_terms.meaning: India's annual statement of allocations benefiting women.
A husband ruling in his elected wife's name.
A feature of NEP 2020.
Periodic Labour Force Survey, which tracks participation annually.
The source for unpaid work in the Indian context.

worked_example.title: Apply the three priority questions
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a loan scheme for women. The deck says that if you can ask only three checklist questions, ask about control, disaggregated targets and accountability.
steps: Control: is the loan used by her? Ask who decided its use and who operates the account.
Disaggregated targets: set targets for women's share of borrowers and for outcomes as well as reports.
Accountability: name a senior person responsible, with sign-off.
Write the answers into the design document and not a separate annex.
worked_example.answer: Three answers on control, targets and accountability, written into the design.

mistakes: Treating the Gender Budget Statement as verified spending.
Citing MGNREGA as a live scheme without checking its current status.
Reading a reserved seat as authority.
Reporting a reform's gender content without asking who bears its cost.

recall.q: Since when has India's Union Budget carried a Gender Budget Statement?
What is the sarpanch pati problem?
recall.a: Husbands ruling in their elected wives' names.

recall.q: Which reform includes a Gender Inclusion Fund?
Which survey tracks labour-force participation annually?
What are the three questions to ask if you can only ask three?
recall.a: Control, disaggregated targets and who is accountable.

notes.2: Use the agenda to plan your reading. Sections 1 and 2 give the definition and concepts, sections 3 and 4 the frameworks and analysis, sections 5 to 7 the cycle, budgets and indicators, and sections 8 to 11 the twin track, institutions, critiques and India.
notes.4: The definition reads as a legal text, so take it clause by clause: assess implications for women and men, of any planned action, in all areas and levels. Equality is the goal and mainstreaming is the strategy. The last clause names four stages, and **three of them are where mainstreaming usually stops**.
notes.5: Beijing 1995 made mainstreaming the agreed strategy across 12 critical areas, adopted by 189 governments. It creates a political commitment with no treaty force. Read your country's five-yearly review beside the **shadow reports from women's organisations**, since the gap between them is usually the most informative document.
notes.6: Run the deletion test on any proposal: remove the gender paragraph and see whether anything else changes. If nothing moves, **gender was an annex**. The reverse test also works, since real analysis should change a timing, location, channel or target.
notes.7: A gender-blind design assumes a user with a man's time, mobility and assets, and it excludes whoever does not fit. A toilet block without lockable facilities for women is sanitation for all and **used by almost no women**. Ask who actually turned up, at what hour and from how far.
notes.8: Use the test column to place any programme on the ladder from exploitative to norm-changing. The exploitative category is the one people skip: relying on women's unpaid time counts. Most real programmes are sensitive or responsive, and **claiming the top rung needs a norms objective** and a way to measure norms.
notes.9: Equality of treatment gives everyone the same input, and equity gives input according to need. Mainstreaming uses equity to reach equality. Article 14 guarantees equality and Article 15(3) permits special provision for women and children. CEDAW treats **temporary special measures** as non-discrimination.
notes.10: Frame gender work as an obligation, because CEDAW, the Beijing Platform, SDG 5 and national policy all carry duties. The table lists what each requires. The practical gain is budget: **obligations get budget lines and values get statements**. India ratified CEDAW in 1993 with declarations.
notes.11: Check your team's talk against these myths. Mainstreaming covers more than adding women, more than a separate project, more than a focal point, includes men and never ends. Each myth contains the work by making it small, someone else's or finished. **Name which one you hear.**
notes.13: Sex is biological and gender is social, learned and therefore changeable. The last row of the table is why the distinction matters: gendered outcomes are a **legitimate object of policy**. Be accurate about what a sex column in your data actually measures.
notes.14: Moser names three kinds of women's work: productive, reproductive and community. Two of the three are invisible to the national accounts, which is why **time-use surveys** matter. Use the table to see which kinds are paid and counted in GDP. India's Time Use Survey is the source for unpaid work.
notes.15: Ask whose time a programme spends. Women carry a triple role at once, so a new meeting, training or worksite **displaces something else**, usually rest or a daughter's schooling. A time-use question in the baseline answers what the activity replaces in her day, in one line.
notes.16: Compare the two tables. Practical needs ease the condition and arise from existing roles, and strategic needs change position and meet resistance. Practical needs are legitimate but can reinforce the division of labour. **Good practice pairs them**, such as a water point and a water committee she chairs.
notes.17: Separate condition, her material state, from position, her standing relative to men. A handpump improves condition and a land title shifts position. **State which column your programme occupies**, and avoid calling a handpump empowerment. Lasting equality needs both.
notes.18: Kabeer's empowerment runs from resources to agency to achievements. Resources alone are not empowerment: think of an account she does not operate or a title she cannot sell. Measure each link separately and report where the chain breaks. **'Accounts opened' covers one link.**
notes.19: A woman is never only a woman: caste, class, religion, disability, age and location intersect. **Cross-tabulate** where you might have controlled, because the largest gap usually sits at the intersection. Reporting a gender gap and a caste gap separately hides it. Disability is rarely collected, so it is mostly invisible.
notes.20: Gender is relational, so include men and boys as stakeholders and allies, and recognise transgender and non-binary people. NALSA (2014) recognised a third gender with self-identification, and the Transgender Persons Act followed in 2019 with criticism. The concrete step is **a data field that admits more than two values**.
notes.22: Choose a framework by the question it answers. Harvard maps roles, access and control, Moser looks at needs and the triple role, Kabeer examines institutions, and GAM is participatory. They carry different politics, so **choosing is an analytical decision**. Many teams combine Harvard, Moser and GAM.
notes.23: Use Harvard as a first pass: activity profile, access and control profile, influencing factors. Its strength is a concrete table that a sceptical manager will read, and its limit is that it describes the division of labour without asking why. If women do 80% of water fetching, it suggests **a closer water point**.
notes.24: Moser's framework asks whether a programme only eases life or reshapes power. Read its four questions as design consequences: budget for time, say practical or strategic, say if the division of labour is unchanged, and target the transfer. Applied carefully, it will show that **most of your portfolio meets practical needs**.
notes.25: Kabeer's Social Relations Approach moves the lens from women to institutions: household, market, state and community, analysed through rules, resources, people, activities and power. Reach for it when asking **why a gap persists despite a programme**, because it points at an institution your programme does not touch.
notes.26: GAM is run by the community. Fill a grid of four levels, women, men, household and community, against labour, time, resources and culture. Look for the unexpected negative cell, such as a benefit to women that costs men something or a resource gain that costs time. **Those cells are where backlash starts.**
notes.27: Use the second table to choose: Harvard for the current pattern, Moser for whether power shifts, Kabeer for why it persists, GAM for what the community says. Map first, then interrogate. **The framework you used limits what you can conclude**, so avoid a claim about shifting power on a descriptive framework.
notes.28: Memorise the four questions: who does what, who has what, who decides, who benefits. They are the portable core of gender analysis. The data table shows what answers each one. **The third and fourth get skipped**, because they need survey questions or conversations you did not budget for.
notes.30: Gender analysis is a systematic examination done before the design is fixed, grounded in data and voices, and predictive about effects. An analysis commissioned after approval can only annotate. If asked for one on a finished design, **say what it can and cannot do**, because that sentence is more useful than the analysis.
notes.31: This chart is illustrative. Its point is that an average of 70% covered can hide men at 85% and women at 55%. Disaggregating every indicator by sex is step zero. **You cannot manage a gap you cannot see**, and the headline number is where gaps hide.
notes.32: Sex-disaggregated data splits indicators you already measure, and gender data measures gendered issues such as unpaid care, violence, mobility and agency. Both are necessary. **Collection method is part of the definition**: a survey given to the household head in front of family will not produce accurate data on violence.
notes.33: Run any intervention through the four questions, and study the common wrong answers in the table. Each treats the household as a single unit with one set of interests. **Ask about individuals in your baseline**: whose name is on the title differs from whether the family owns land.
notes.34: Access is the opportunity to use a resource, and control is the power to decide over it. The table lists five typical cases, such as farming land in his name. The indicator has to reach one step further: **accounts operated by the account-holder** and who decided how a loan was used.
notes.35: Read the grid with access on one axis and control on the other. Mainstreaming pushes resources toward the top-right quadrant, which has both. Place your own beneficiaries in the four boxes. Note the **access-without-control box**, where she farms land she cannot sell.
notes.36: Use the minimum viable version of each step. It is a few days of work and a full study is unnecessary. Run women's and men's focus groups separately, since mixed groups produce the men's account of the division of labour. Cost is rarely why it does not happen: **nobody is accountable for it**.
notes.38: Gender belongs at every stage, and a gap at any stage leaks the gains made at the others. The table gives the gender question and the leak for each stage. The commonest gap sits between design and implementation. **Monitoring is where a leak can still be fixed**, for example in month three.
notes.39: Set explicit gender objectives at design, because design is where mainstreaming is won or lost. Ordinary choices have predictable gendered effects: meeting time, location, staff, information channel and eligibility documents. **Documentation is the quiet exclusion**, since a scheme keyed to a land title or an account in one's own name excludes the people it names.
notes.40: Pair each delivery barrier with its fix. Childcare has the clearest evidence and the lowest adoption. The slide uses MGNREGA's crèche provision as an example of uneven implementation, then notes that the Act was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced, so **check the current provision** before you cite it.
notes.41: Disaggregate every output and outcome by sex, and add indicators on control, voice and workload. The table pairs level, indicator and trap: counting heads, household-level reporting, unasked agency and slow norms. **Build disaggregation into the MIS at the start**, since retrofitting after two years costs a data migration.
notes.42: A gender marker turns 'is this gender-sensitive?' into a portfolio score. Its weakness is self-assignment at design with little audit, and several evaluations found systematic over-scoring. Even so, assigning a score **forces someone to ask what the design does about gender** before approval.
notes.43: Apply the score test: 0 if no analysis informed the design, 1 if analysis changed something concrete, 2 if the project would not exist without the gender objective. A maternal-health programme scores 2 only if it aims to change gendered outcomes. Watch the red flag: **many 1s and almost no 2s**.
notes.44: Counting heads is a weak measure of participation. Use the ladder, nominal, present, voice, influence and authority, to decide in advance which level you aim at and how you will know. Watch **proxy participation**, such as a husband attending for his wife, which most systems record as her participation.
notes.45: Plan for backlash as a programme risk: anticipate reactions, engage men and family before the transfer, avoid publishing names or amounts, hold a referral route and ask in private whether anything changed. The evidence is mixed, and **the design implication is the same: anticipate it**.
notes.47: GRB analyses the whole budget, revenue as well as expenditure, and works as a restructuring question without being a separate women's budget. The revenue half is nearly always omitted, though indirect taxes fall harder on households where women control small budgets. **Check that your exercise changes allocations** and is more than a report.
notes.48: Policies promise and budgets deliver, so a gender policy without money is a wish. GRB is how mainstreaming reaches the stage that decides what happens: **the allocation of resources**. Ask of any policy where the money line sits.
notes.49: Sort spending into three buckets: women-specific, pro-equality within general, and general. The radical step is the third bucket, the supposedly neutral majority. The deck's arithmetic is that **a gender-blind general allocation outweighs** anything achievable in the first. Ask what the largest programme does to gendered outcomes.
notes.50: Read India's Gender Budget Statement carefully: Part A has 100% allocation for women and girls, Part B at least 30%, and since 2024-25 Part C lists pro-women schemes below 30%. It rests on ministry self-reporting and no audit. It is still an advance, because it created **an annual public number to argue about**.
notes.51: This chart is an illustrative shape and does not show actual figures. The recurring real-world finding the deck cites is that the gender share hovers at a small single-digit percentage and barely grows. Use the chart to compare **ambition with allocation**, then look up the real figures.
notes.52: Most spending that decides a woman's day sits below the union budget, in state departments, panchayats and municipalities. A gender budget confined to the centre misses it. Local budgeting lets women weigh in on a handpump, a lit bus stop or a crèche. **Kerala's Women Component Plan** is the case cited.
notes.53: Walk the five steps in order: profile, assess policy, check the budget matches, track spending by gender, reassess. Most efforts stop at step 3. **Step 4 is the hinge**, because without expenditure tracking by gender the first three steps produce a document and no accountability. The framework is Budlender and Sharp's.
notes.54: Check four failures: reporting after the fact, mislabelling general schemes, allocation without release and no outcome link. Compare budget estimates, revised estimates and actuals for gender-tagged lines. **A large gap between first and last** is the commonest failure. Mislabelling lets you say the gender budget grew while nothing changed.
notes.56: Good indicators make invisible change visible without flattening it. Use the bridge column: most 'unmeasurable' outcomes have a measurable proxy, but nobody specified one. Pair numbers with qualitative evidence. Watch the corollary: **what is easy to measure gets over-funded** relative to what matters.
notes.57: Measure three layers: access or condition, agency, and position or norms. They move at different speeds: months, years, decades. Three-year projects often report on the first layer and **claim the third**. Choose the layer your horizon can reach, and state what your theory of change assumes about the rest.
notes.58: Use NFHS agency questions to benchmark against a real population figure and avoid inventing a baseline. They cover healthcare, major purchases, visits to family, phone use and an account she uses herself. The account question separates having one from using it, which is **access versus control made operational**.
notes.59: This chart is illustrative, patterned on kinds of gaps in regional data, and its bars are not exact statistics. The deck says the pattern is real: women trail on participation, assets and control across South Asia. Use it to prompt the question, then **pull the real data** for your setting.
notes.60: Measure violence only with GBV-sensitive methods: private interviews, trained women interviewers, one woman per household, referral information ready and no village-level reporting. These are WHO recommendations because the research can endanger respondents. **A fall in reported cases** may mean less safety in reporting, and the data cannot tell which.
notes.61: Composite indices such as the UNDP GII and the WEF Gender Gap Index suit advocacy and comparison over time. The WEF index measures gaps and leaves out levels, so a poor country can rank above a rich one. **Open the index back up** before drawing a programme conclusion from a rank.
notes.62: Test each indicator against five properties: disaggregable, relevant, sensitive, ethical and feasible. Sensitivity is the one most often missing. Ask what value the indicator would take if the programme succeeded and what if it failed. **If the two are close, replace it.**
notes.63: Weave numbers and stories. The number says accounts opened rose, and the story says whether she operates the account. Most Significant Change and outcome harvesting are the usual named methods. **Collect qualitative data before you know the quantitative result**, or the stories become illustrations of a conclusion already reached.
notes.65: Run two tracks together, because mainstreaming alone dilutes into nothing and women-only projects alone stay marginal. Track 1 integrates gender everywhere, and Track 2 targets specific gaps. The deck calls the approach standard in EU, UN and most donor policy, so **cite policy when a proposal is challenged**.
notes.66: Read the diagram as two inputs to one goal. Mainstreaming spreads the lens everywhere, and targeting closes the gaps that mainstreaming alone leaves. Redraw it for your organisation, with your programmes under each track, and see **which track is empty**.
notes.67: Read the two columns as mirror images: each track's failure is the other track's function. Mainstreaming alone becomes everyone's job and so no one's, and targeting alone stays a silo. The gender unit needs **a portfolio of its own and a mandate** over everyone else's.
notes.68: These examples show what only targeting can do: SHGs build collective agency, scholarships close an enrolment gap, women-only skilling reaches excluded women, and reserved seats put women in decision-making at scale. Beware **enclosure**, where all gender work gets sent to Track 2.
notes.69: One women's project does not mean gender is done. Track 2 is necessary and never sufficient. If your only gender work is a separate women's component, **you are doing Track 2**, and the mainstream itself still has to change. Ask what else in the portfolio has changed.
notes.70: Set the mix by context. Where gaps are wide and voice is weak, Track 2 may lead to build agency, and Track 1 then opens the mainstream. Think of Track 2 as **capability** and Track 1 as **opportunity**. Empowerment without opportunity frustrates, and opportunity without capability excludes.
notes.71: Add a third strand of work with men and boys on shared care, respectful relationships and harmful masculinities, because women's gains stick only when norms around men shift. Watch the live risk in the table: **men becoming the visible voice** of gender work. The common feature of programmes that work is sustained group work.
notes.72: Hold the one-line summary: mainstream gender into everything and keep the targeted work that only women's empowerment can do. **Mainstreaming without targeting drifts, and targeting without mainstreaming stalls.** Use it as a closing test on any portfolio you review.
notes.74: Institutionalised means gender survives the departure of the committed individual. Check five layers with the table's tests: a policy that blocks approval, an MIS that refuses undisaggregated records, trained managers, a budget line and a culture that outlasts the champion. Most organisations claiming this have **hired one committed person**.
notes.75: A gender policy changes nothing on the shelf. Wire it into the gateways: no gender analysis, no approval. Use procurement and partnership criteria, **the most underused lever**, since grantees produce what you require. A policy that cannot block an approval is a statement of intent.
notes.76: Capacity needs training for all staff, required tools, time in the workplan, a budget and an accountable person. **Time is the shortfall nobody costs.** Training alone has a poor record and works when paired with a tool people must use and a decision point where it is checked.
notes.77: A focal point should advise, build capacity and hold the portfolio view. The trap is a junior woman with the title and no authority, time or budget. Two fixes work: **write the role into the job description with time allocated**, and give the post-holder formal sign-off in approvals.
notes.78: Rank the mechanisms: targets in performance plans, mandatory disaggregated reporting, marker tracking and consequences tied to results. The first three produce information, and **only the fourth changes behaviour**, which is almost never implemented. A useful step is to make marker distribution public inside the organisation by department.
notes.79: A gender audit turns the lens inward, as a participatory self-assessment pioneered in the ILO model, with staff assessing their own organisation. Its value depends on what follows, so **fix a management response and a follow-up date** before you start. The table lists typical findings.
notes.80: Culture is the hardest layer, but much of it leaves a record: who is credited in minutes, gender ratio by grade, meeting times and complaints. Treat it as measurable. In India the POSH Act requires an Internal Committee and annual reporting for qualifying workplaces, so **you can ask for that document**.
notes.81: Staff calibrate effort to what leadership asks about. One senior person asking the disaggregation question in every review does more than a training programme. If leadership does not ask, **no focal point compensates**. Use the table to read your own leaders' signals.
notes.83: Three decades on, mainstreaming is near-universal in policy language and patchy in practice. The five critiques are distinct diagnoses with distinct remedies. Evaporation and capacity failures are fixable with resources and accountability, while the critiques of the frame itself **cannot be fixed by better implementation**. Work out which applies.
notes.84: Longwe's image is commitment evaporating like water in heat as it passes down the bureaucracy. The table shows five handovers where gender content can be lost without anyone deciding to drop it. The counter is **a named person and a check at each handover**.
notes.85: Tokenism keeps the form and drains the substance: a gender paragraph, a photograph of women, a quota met on paper. Ask what it changed and whether it is measured and reported. The form survives because it is what gets checked, so **changing what the template checks** is the lever.
notes.86: The depoliticisation critique says tools, checklists and markers strip out the political core, since gender equality is about power. The tools made the agenda adoptable by removing what made it contentious. **Keep the power question inside the tool**, such as 'who decides and who loses' beside 'how many women attended'.
notes.87: Co-option shows in language shifts: women to gender, rights to efficiency, movements to stakeholders, patriarchy to gender relations. The efficiency argument works with finance ministries and can be defeated by evidence about payoff. **Know whether you are making a rights argument or an instrumental one**, and say which.
notes.88: These practical failures have cheap structural fixes: a mandatory checklist, a budget line, a required MIS field and sign-off authority for the focal point. None needs a change of attitude, so push for them first. **Attitude follows structure**, because people who answer the four questions at approval learn to ask them earlier.
notes.89: Expect resistance, open and quiet: 'gender is Western', 'our women are content', 'this divides the family'. The table pairs each with a response. The imported-agenda claim is answerable with domestic law and the women's movement. **Quiet non-compliance is more common** and is beaten by verification.
notes.90: Keep mainstreaming honest by keeping power in the frame, resourcing it or admitting it is rhetoric, tracking outcomes and keeping women's movements at the table. The fourth is **the structural safeguard against co-option**. Treat critique as course-correction. The goal is a fairer distribution of power.
notes.92: Use the table to find the hook for any demand you make: the Constitution (Articles 14, 15, 16, 39, 42), the Ministry of Women and Child Development, the Gender Budget Statement since 2005-06, the 73rd and 74th Amendments, and laws such as POSH. The puzzle is **dense machinery with uneven outcomes**.
notes.93: Place each flagship scheme on a track: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and DAY-NRLM are targeted, PM Ujjwala meets practical needs, and MGNREGA carries a 33% share for women inside a mainstream scheme. The gap is in strategic needs: land, voice and safety. **The slide treats MGNREGA as current**, so check its status.
notes.94: Test each reform with one question: does it shift women's position or only adjust condition, and who was at the table? NEP 2020 has a Gender Inclusion Fund, the labour codes cover maternity, equal remuneration and night work, and the 2017 maternity amendment shows how **the cost of a measure shapes behaviour**.
notes.95: India's most-discussed gap is women's low and long-stagnant labour-force participation, with a recent uptick driven largely by rural self-employment. This chart is an illustrative shape and does not show PLFS figures. PLFS tracks the series annually, so **pull the real numbers** before you quote any.
notes.96: Reservation put over a million women into local government, with real and contested results. Watch the sarpanch pati problem: **a seat is access, and real decision-making is control**. The research shows investment shifting toward women's priorities and attitudes easing over time, but effects vary by state.
notes.97: Use the twelve questions as a design review. If you can ask only three, ask about control, disaggregated targets and who is accountable. The table lists the items most often skipped. **Write your answers into the design document** and avoid a separate annex, so implementers read them.
notes.98: Read at least one critique alongside the frameworks, because a practitioner who knows only the tools applies them competently to the wrong question. Start with Moser for method, Kabeer for empowerment, Beijing for the frame, and Razavi and Miller or Rao and Kelleher for critique. **NFHS, the Time Use Survey and PLFS** give free Indian data.
notes.99: Take these five tests into any meeting: delete the gender paragraph, ask who can sell and keep the income, say practical or strategic, ask what exists besides the women's project, and ask who decides and who loses. **If you take one, take the first.**
